translation:
_Kari sanmaan aasan mohe deeno. Kaahaa daan tohe deeje. Swaarathke hum naahi lobhiye. Bhakti daan mohe deeje. ||2||_ (He honored me and gave me a seat, asking what gift He should give me. I said I am not greedy for selfish gain — give me the gift of devotion.)

_Pakri baanhe bheetar mohi leena. Sab asthaan deekhlaavaa. Naam nighant tilak aur maalaa. Daas Kabir pehnaavaa. ||3||_ (He caught my arm and drew me inside, and showed me every place; and from the whole treasury of His names He adorned this servant Kabir with His name, with tilak, and with a garland.)

Daas Kabirji says: I, a guest of the Lord, sang His pure, glorious hymns and kirtans in praise of His fame, and sang the glory of the lotus feet of Ram. To a devotee the Lord surely grants fearlessness — He came bearing the gift of surrender and dedication for His devotee. The Lord was resting in His palace; this servant-devotee went there and sang the Lord's praises. Hearing this, the Lord woke with a start and understood that some devotee-servant had come to Him with an earnest plea. The Lord honored me, welcomed me, gave me a seat, and asked what boon He should give me. I said I was not greedy for selfish gain; grant me instead the boon of devotion to You. The Lord took hold of my hand and called me inside, and from all the words in His treasury of names He adorned this devotee Kabir with His own name, with tilak (of gopichandan), and with a garland of tulsi beads.

Thus Kabirji too reached all the way to the Lord's palace, and so he says—

_Kabir dahlikee to sab koi kahai. Mahalkee na kahai koy. Mahalkee to tab kahai. Jo mahalkaa mahrami hoy._ (Kabir says: everyone can speak of the entrance-hall, but none can speak of the palace itself. Only one who is intimate with the palace, familiar with its inner secret, can speak of the palace.)

Daas Kabirji says that everyone can talk about the threshold at the entrance of a royal palace, but no one can describe the beauty of its interior. That inner splendor of the palace can be told only by someone who is an intimate insider, familiar with its private secret.

The dahli (entrance-hall) is the Lord's outer court, the illusion (maya) of creation, while the mahal (palace) is the Supreme Being's highest abode. The dahli is ritual, desire-bound worship; the mahal is the inner soul's desireless, loving devotion.

_Naadi vaadi bahu milai. Karat kaleje chhed. (Koi) takht talekaa naa milaa. Jaason poochhoon bhed._ (One meets many who merely chant or merely argue, wounding the heart with disputation; but none is found who sits beneath the throne, of whom I might ask the secret.)

Daas Kabirji says: those who merely worship the unstruck sound, and mere talkers — scholars of the Vedas, well-versed in the scriptures, given to disputation — one meets many such people, then and now, who are the sort that wound the heart and cut into it. But no one is found who reveals the secret of the highest truth of loving devotion, of whom one could ask the secret of peace and supreme bliss.

_Takht talekaa so kahai. Jo takht talekaa hoy. Maanjh mahalkee ko kahai. Padadaa gaadhaa soy._ (He alone can speak of what lies beneath the throne who himself is beneath the throne; and who can speak of the very heart of the palace, so thick is the veil there.)

Daas Kabirji says only one who is the Lord's own servant, devotee, and attendant can speak of the vision of the Supreme Being — but to enter, to penetrate into the palace (the inner being) of the Imperishable One is rare; no ordinary person can gain entry there, for the knot of maya's veil surrounds it.

_Maanjh mahalkee guru kahai. Dekhaa sab nij gharbaar. Poonji deenhee hoth kar. Padadaa diyaa dathaay._ (Only the guru can speak of the very heart of the palace, for he has seen all of his own house; he has placed the treasure in hand and torn away the veil.)

Daas Kabirji says only the Guru can speak of the highest abode, for he has seen and experienced the Lord's court — the house of loving devotion, the inner soul — and its treasure of singular devotion. Having given, through the key of his guidance in devotion, all that is his, he has thrown open the veil of maya, of ritual and the rest.

_Shobhaa hai darbaarkee. Prataap Daas Kabir. Panth puraatan khojke. Door kiyaa pad cheer._ (The splendor is that of His court, by the glory of Daas Kabir; having searched out the ancient path, he has torn away and cast off the veil.)

Gnaniji Maharaj says: by the glory of Daas Kabirji the standing of the royal assembly of the Lord's court, the assembly of loving devotion, has grown. He sought out the old, original path of loving devotion and tore away the tattered veil of maya such as ritual.

It is said in the Samagam that Kabir and Narsinh Mehta had one and the same guru, and it has first been explained who and what kind of guru Narsinh Mehta had.

|| Godi ||

_Bhai re mune Hari gaavaani (bhajavaani) tev padi. Maaharaa Shaamaliaane na mooku ek ghadi. Ghailun man maaharun alagu rahi na shake re. Maahare saachi Harisu preet jadi. ||tek|| ||1||_ (O brother, I have grown so used to worshipping Hari that I shall not leave my dark-hued Lord even for a moment. My maddened mind cannot bear to stay apart even an instant — my love has truly become fused with Hari.)

_Aakhaa divasno rali khapi aavyo. Bhaabhiye naa mookyun paani. Men jaanyun tun veranaa maari. Bhaabhi notaa goraani. ||2||_ (Having spent the whole day occupied in worldly business, I came home, but my sister-in-law did not give me water for my bath. I understood: you are indeed my adversary, sister-in-law, not truly a gentle lady.)

_Men jaanyun Dhruvni pere karu re. Naamdevjinaa chhaapraa chhaahi aapyaan. Kabirjine apichal vaani. Evun jaani rose bhataano. Mune chhabilaji mookse paani. ||3||_ (I resolved to do as Dhruv did. He who thatched Namdevji's roof, and gave Kabirji everlasting speech of devotion — knowing this, I grew angry, resolved that my beautiful Lord too will surely give me water,)

_Te pe hun hoees bhalero._ (and thereby I too shall become blessed.)

_Evaan vachan suni Narsaiyaanaan. Bhaabhi bolyaan vaani. Uthho devariaa hun suti huti. Tatkshan mahelyun paani. ||4||_ (Hearing such words from Narsaiya, the sister-in-law spoke: "Get up, brother-in-law, I was asleep" — and at once she brought water.)

_Ghan Vrindaavan ghan Jamunaa tar. Dhan Raadhaa Rukmini raani. Dhan dhan Narsaiyaani jeebhaladi. Je jape chhabilaa Saarang paani. ||5||_ (Blessed is Vrindavan, blessed the bank of the Yamuna; blessed is Queen Radha, blessed Rukmini. Blessed, blessed is Narsaiya's tongue, which chants the name of the beautiful Sarangpani.)

_Kathan kaaraj mune bhaabhiye deedhun. Reesaai gayo van mojhaar. Ugra tap men vanmen saadhyo. Dayaa kari mane Tripuraari. ||6||_ (My sister-in-law set me a hard task; angered, I went off into the forest. There I performed severe austerity, and Tripurari showed me mercy.)

_Gopeshware kahun Narsaiyaa. Je maage te aapo tune. Men kahun prabhu tamne vahalu. Kriyaa karine aapo mune. ||7||_ (Gopeshwar said, "Narsaiya, ask, and whatever you ask I shall grant you." I said, "O Lord, whatever is dear to You — grant that to me, in true act.")

_Bholaa chakravat prasann thayaa. Tatkshan aavi graho haath. Sol sahasra gopivar ramataa. Te raas dekhaadyo jyaan Vaikunthnaath. ||8||_ (The innocent, discus-bearing Lord was pleased, and at once came and took hold of my hand. He showed me the raas-dance where the Lord of Vaikuntha sported among sixteen thousand chief gopis.)

_Shri Vrajbhaanu Nandlaalaa. Sakhi samaani sarve saath. Param kripaal dayaal heet kaaran. Deepak dharaabyo maare haath. ||9||_ (Radha, daughter of Vrajbhanu, was with Nandlal, together with all the gopi companions. The supremely gracious, merciful Lord, for love's sake, placed a lamp in my hand.)

_Het kari mune deekshaa deedhi. Kripaanaath Lakshmi bharathaar. E re Narsaiyaa tun leelaa gaaje. Je keedhi Krishna avataar. ||10||_ (Out of love He gave me initiation — the merciful Lord, husband of Lakshmi. "O Narsaiya, now proclaim the divine play that I performed in the Krishna incarnation.")

Ah, brother, I have grown so used to worshipping the Lord that now I shall not let go of my devotion to Krishna even for one moment. My mind has become so restless that it cannot bear separation from your devotion even slightly. My love has truly become fused with the Lord. One day, after being occupied all day with worldly business, I came home, and my sister-in-law did not give me water for my bath. I thought: this one, who ought to hold me in the highest love, is not behaving like a real sister-in-law but like a guru's wife truly teaching me a lesson. I thought: let me too, like Dhruvji did when he was humiliated, perform such devotion. The Lord who thatched Namdevji's roof, and who gave Kabirji the excellent gift of devotional speech — hymn, kirtan, couplet — understanding that the Lord is such a gracious giver, I grew angry, thinking that the beautiful Lord will give water to me too, and thereby I shall be blessed. Hearing such words from my Narsaiya, my sister-in-law spoke thus: "O my brother-in-law, I was only being neglectful, I was speaking carelessly" — and she at once brought water. Blessed is Vrindavan, blessed is the bank of the river Yamuna, and blessed too are Radhaji and Rukmini; blessed too is the tongue of Narsinh Mehta, which performs such devotion, which recites this hymn and kirtan of devotion to the beautiful Lord.

My sister-in-law spoke harsh words to me, so, angered, I went off into the forest; there I performed nine days of severe, intense austerity, and Shivji showed mercy on me. Gopeshwar Mahadev said, "O Narsinh Mehta, whatever is dear to you, ask it of me graciously." The innocent, good Lord Krishna, bearer of the Sudarshan discus, was pleased, and at once took hold of my hand — that is, called me to Him — and showed me the raas dance being played by the Lord, the very husband of sixteen thousand gopi-queens. Radha, daughter of Vrishabhanu, was there with Nanda's son Krishna, along with all the other gopi companions. That most excellent, gracious Lord, in order to show me mercy, made me hold a lamp in my hand and showed me the raas, and said to me, "O Narsinh, now describe and sing in kirtan what I have shown you — the very sport I performed at the time of my Krishna incarnation."

Narsinh Mehta received just one rebuke from his sister-in-law, and through it was granted the vision of the Lord's raas; he had performed austerity with true inner sincerity and thereby pleased Gopeshwar. This shows that when a person is deeply struck by such a rebuke, and cultivates intense feeling through lament, and becomes resolutely determined to accomplish the task, then his boat crosses over — his task succeeds. Adhyaruji says that if we, in this same way, become firmly resolved and take the Lord's name with true intent, performing devotion, then we shall attain God. If one does not take the Lord's name with dread and intense fervor, calling on His name, how then can the Lord be pleased? There have been many such instances where people, roused by just one such rebuke, attained God or accomplished their task.

Bhaktimarg, Year 1, Issue 1, page 186, 1-28: It is said that when Tulsidas's wife saw Tulsidas maddened after her, she gave him a rebuke:

_Haad chaam may deh mam, taam par jitni preeti. Tisu aadhi jo Raam prati, avasi mitahi bhavbheeti._ ("As much love as you bear for this body of mine, made of bone and flesh — if you bore even half of that for Shri Ramchandra, all the fear of this worldly existence would surely vanish.")

O lord, this decaying, unclean body of flesh and bone — the love you hold for it, if you were to hold even half of that love for Shri Ramchandraji, then every trace of fear of this world would be destroyed — because of this, Tulsidas became a great devotee of Ram.

2. The great devotee of Shri Krishna, Surdas, too, was once caught in infatuation for a courtesan named Chintamani. Then Chintamani herself gave him just such a rebuke: that just as he day and night meditated only on her, and did not even care for his body in seeking to attain her, in the very same way, if he meditated on the Supreme Being with a single mind, and did not care even for his life in doing so, his liberation would come about easily. Surdasji's eyes, which had been asleep in infatuation, were opened by this rebuke, and he became absorbed wholly in devotion to Lord Krishna.

3. The child-devotee Dhruvji, too, was awakened by just such a rebuke from his stepmother: "O son, in this very birth you shall not be able to sit on your father's lap, for you are the son of an unfortunate woman; only if you perform devotion and take birth from my own womb will you become entitled to sit on your father's lap." By this rebuke, at the mere age of five, performing austerity for just six months, he pleased Lord Vishnu and obtained a long reign of royal happiness and the imperishable abode.

4. Narsinh Mehta, too, pleased the Lord through just such a rebuke.

5. A wealthy merchant of Bengal was standing on his porch one evening to buy milk. While taking milk from the milkmaid, he fell into some conversation. The milkmaid gave him a rebuke: "Sheth, you seem to be idle. Just look at the day — the sun is about to set, and I still have far to go." It occurred to him: "Must I too go far, to the other world, and how much longer is it before my own sunset, my own death, comes?" So he left there and went to Vrindavan. There, with his own wealth, he built a temple and lived there performing bhajan; that temple, called Lala Babu's temple, still exists today.

There is also another folk-tale about him: that boatmen on the far bank of the Hooghly river, calling out to people to cross into the city, would shout that evening was falling and this was the very last trip they would take with the boat, so anyone wishing to cross should get in now. By this same rebuke, the temple he had built still exists today as well.

6. A similar incident is that of Saprū Sahib, the English Collector of Itarsi. The barber who used to massage his feet told him a tale: that in the kingdom of Balkh, a maidservant once fell asleep on the king's bed, for which she was sentenced to a hundred lashes. The maidservant said, "I slept on the bed for only ten minutes, and for that a hundred lashes fell on me — then how many would fall on one who sleeps on it permanently?" By this rebuke, that very king became a fakir. Hearing this tale, Collector Saprū too became a sadhu, and came to live in the city of Itawa as a wandering mendicant.

When he grew old, he would go out begging with a stick, and the tapping sound of the stick made a "khat-khat" noise, so people called him "Khatkhata Baba."

7. A similar incident occurred at the death, on the battlefield, of Uday Mehta, the minister of Siddharaj. This Uday Mehta was a Jain; when wounded, he expressed his final wish to have the darshan of a yati (Jain monk). Where could a yati be found on a battlefield? But a soldier brought along an acquaintance, a folk-actor, having dressed him in the garb of a yati. That folk-actor-turned-yati said "Dharma labh," and thereby Uday Mehta's wish was fulfilled, and he died content. Because of this, that folk-actor became, permanently, a true yati.

8. The poet Kalidas was a great fool. Once, a king's son fell ill on the way to his wedding, so in his place an ordinary man had to be made the bridegroom; thus the handsome but foolish Kalidas was made the counterfeit groom. In the bedchamber, the learned princess to whom he had been married, wishing to make sweet conversation with him, asked Kalidas whether he had any words of wit and charm. By this rebuke, Kalidas performed worship of the Goddess Mother and became a great scholar, writing three great epic poems on those very three words, and thus turned from a great fool into a great scholar.

9. Panini, too, was a great fool, so his teacher called him a bullock. So he went and sat by the bull-image in a temple of Shiva, and pleased Shiva, and became a great scholar; he wrote the famous Sanskrit grammar.

10. This is from my own life's experience. I went to Radhnathbhai Laldas of Dhoda, who, together with Trikam Gordhan, had published a garba-book named "Bhakt Bhavamrut" that criticized the revered Yadunathji, to tell him to withdraw it. Radhnathbhai agreed to withdraw it and invited me to dine. I said that just then I had a recitation engagement at the home of devotee Parag Vrundavan of Kandevar in Bodeli Gin, so I had to eat there, but that tomorrow, on my way back, I would eat at his place. Tempted by wanting to secure the book, I went to Dhoda, but through Trikam's persuasion Radhnathbhai changed his mind and refused to withdraw the book; then I refused to eat there. His younger brother Haribhai Laldas urged me not to go hungry; I said I would not even drink water in this village that day. He then invited me to eat at his own home, but I still refused; at that he spoke a couplet:

_Sant bade paramaarthi. Shitam jinkaa ang. Orokee tapat boojhaayke. De de apnaa rang._ (Great saints are ones devoted to others' good, whose very bodies are cool; quenching others' burning heat, they give of their own coolness.)

By this rebuke I softened, and went and ate at Haribhai's home, and then returned home. The meaning is that just one such rebuke is enough to awaken a person; many such instances occur in this world. Draupadi's rebuke — "the blind man's son is blind" — led, among other things, to the Mahabharata war.

Narsinh Mehta reached, in devotion, as high a rank as possible as master of the palace, counting his own sister-in-law as his guru. Now, who Kabirji's guru is has been shown through Kabirji's own composition.

|| Raag Prabhaati ||

_Men (us) daure jaaungaa. To men bohor na bhavjal aaungaa. ||men daure|| ||tatek||_ (I shall go to that chosen place; then I shall never again come into this ocean of worldly existence.)

_Soot bohot kachhu thoraa. Taathe kanthaa laai le doraa. Us laaelau kanth horaa. Kanthaa (su) doraa laagaa. (Tab) taathe jaraa maran bhay bhaagaa. ||men daure|| ||1||_ (Thread — some much, some little — with it, take up the patchwork quilt and stitch it. That quilt has been given whole. Once the thread has caught in the quilt, then the fear of old age and death flees from it.)

_Sannihit puni tahaan kanthaa sanahee poonee. Taanhaan base ek muni. Us munisu man lagaaugaa. To men bohor na bhau jal aaungaa. ||2||_ (There, close by the quilt, lies the carded cotton-thread; there dwells a sage. I shall fix my mind on that sage; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

_Meru dand ek chhaajaa. Taanhaan raaj karat (basat) ek raajaa. Us raajaasun chit laaungaa. To men bohor na bhav jal aaungaa. ||3||_ (The spinal column stands there like a single canopy; there a king reigns. I shall fix my heart on that king; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

_Taanhaan soor na ooge chandaa. Taanhaan dekhaa ek aanandaa. Us aanandsu chit lagaaungaa. Taathe men bohor na bhavjal aaungaa. ||4||_ (There neither sun nor moon rises; there I saw only bliss. I shall fix my heart on that bliss; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

_Taanhaan bahu heeraa dhan motee. Taanhaan tattva laai le joti. Taanhaan base prem joti. Us jotsu jot meelaaungaa. Taathe me bohor na bhavaanal aaungaa. ||5||_ (There are many precious jewels, wealth, pearls; there the light of the essential truth has been brought; there dwells the light of love. I shall merge my light with that light; then I shall never again come into the fire of worldly existence.)

_Ek Triveni trat teeraa. Taanhaan adhar amoolak heeraa. Us heerasu het laaungaa. Taathe men bohor na bhavjal aaungaa. ||6||_ (There is one bank of the Triveni confluence; there hangs an unsupported, priceless jewel. I shall fix my love on that jewel; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

_Taanhaan mool tattva ek paavaa. Taanhaan seedh Ganes rahaavaa. Us moole moole melaaungaa. Taathe men bohor na bhavjal aaungaa. ||7||_ (There the one root essence has been found; there the perfected sages and Ganesh dwell. I shall merge root with root there; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

_Kabir taalab teraa. Taathe (taanhaan) gop Hari guru meraa. Men (us) heet (su) Hari chit laaungaa. Taathe men bohor na bhavjal aaungaa. ||8||_ (Kabir, that is your quest; there the cowherd Hari is my guru. I shall fix my heart on that Hari out of love; then I shall never again come into the waters of worldly existence.)

Daas Kabirji says: I shall go, with single-minded resolve, to such an excellent, firmly determined place, and then I shall not come again and again, taking birth in the four wombs, into the waters of this world's ocean of existence. With the little thread of remembrance that I have, I shall stitch it into the patchwork quilt of loving devotion and sew it up. Once the thread of remembrance and worship has been stitched into this quilt of loving devotion, the fear of birth, old age, and death has departed. There, near the quilt of devotion, dwells a holy saint; I shall fix my mind on that saint, and therefore I shall not come again and again into the waters of this world's ocean of existence. The spinal column serves there as a chief support, like a central pole, where a fitting single essence pervades; there a king rules the kingdom of Ram. If I fix my heart on the loving devotion of that king, I shall not come again and again into the water of birth-and-death of this ocean of existence.

In His abode neither sun nor moon rises, but there is only the happiness of the bliss of loving devotion. If I fix my mind on such bliss of loving devotion, I shall not need to come again and again into this water of birth-and-death of the ocean of existence. In that abode there are great saint-devotees, precious like diamonds and pearls, where the light of the essence of loving devotion has been brought and shines. I too shall join my own loving devotion with that light of loving devotion, and therefore I shall not need to come again and again into this water of birth-and-death of the ocean of existence. There is a bank where the confluence of the tilak, the tulsi, the company of saints, and the Lord's name flows as a stream of loving devotion; and beneath that stream lies the very precious jewel of the Lord's name; I shall fix my mind on that jewel of the Lord's name, and so I shall not need to come again and again into this water of birth-and-death of the ocean of existence.

There, I found the root, the fundamental principle at the origin of this creation, in which perfected beings, Ganesh and other gods, indeed all souls, dwell under its shelter. I shall merge my own root soul-essence with that root divine essence, and so I shall not need to come again and again into this water of birth-and-death of the ocean of existence. Kabirji says: O Kabir, you have such an intense yearning, a longing, to search out and attain this excellent place, and so the cowherds and cowherdesses, and the Lord, are my gurus. I shall lovingly fix my heart upon them, and so I shall not need to come again and again into this water of birth-and-death of the ocean of existence.

Bhaktamaal, Part 2, page 55, in the account of Vrindavan Sudama Kuti, this same theme is also mentioned.

Kabir Dasji accepted Shri Swami Ramanandacharyaji as his initiation-guru, and the gopis as his guru of love. As it is said — _Kabiraa taalib toraa. Tahaan gopi Hari guru moraa. (Gohi 31)_ (Kabir, that is your quest — there, the cowherd Hari is my guru) — it is recorded that once Shri Kabiraji was sitting alone on the bank of the Ganga, repeating "Ram Ram." Meanwhile the Lord too was hiding behind a tree, saying "Kabir-Kabir." And why? Then the Lord answered:

_Man aisaa nirmal bhayaa, jaise Gangaaneer. Peechhe peechhe Hari phirai, kahat Kabir Kabir._ ("My mind has become so pure, like the water of the Ganga, that Hari follows behind me, calling out 'Kabir, Kabir.'")

Hearing this, Kabirdasji said—

_Kabiraa Kabiraa kyoon kahe, jaa Jamunaake teer. Ek gopeeke premmen, bahi gaye koti Kabir. Kaisi premras bheeni aki._ ("Why do you call out 'Kabir, Kabir'? Go to the bank of the Yamuna — there, in love for a single gopi, millions of Kabirs have been swept away. How steeped in the nectar of love that is!")

In Manuscript No. 8, page 84, in Sorath-4, it is said regarding Kabir's quest for a guru:

_Neekalankee guru hum paayaare. Jeenai sudhaapanth bataayaa re. Kabiraa taalab teraa. Hari Parabrahm saaheb meraa._ ("I have found a guru utterly without blemish, who has shown me the path of nectar. Kabir, that is your quest — Hari, the Supreme Brahman, is my Master.")

Daas Kabirji says: I have found a guru — the gopis — utterly without blemish, who has shown me the path of the nectar of love's mark. Kabirji had such an intense longing to attain this kind of devotion, and so my worshipped Lord is Hari, the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Being.

There are many kinds of gurus, so whichever one truly shows devotion is the fitting guru; therefore it has been told in a couplet what kind of disciple a certain kind of guru has, and what kind of guru a certain kind of disciple has.

_Kabir kaamikaa guru kaaminee. Lobheekaa guru daam. Kabirkaa guru bhagat hai. Bhagatanke guru Raam. ||1||_ (Kabir says: the lustful man's guru is a woman; the greedy man's guru is money. Kabir's guru is the devotee; and the devotee's guru is Ram.)

Daas Kabirji says: the object of worship for the lustful is beauty, and for the greedy it is wealth. Likewise, seekers and the pious are saint-devotees, and the goal of saint-devotees is Ram. Thus people of these three kinds of character — the lustful, the greedy, and the devotee — have gurus according to their own respective nature.

_Kabir trividh lok trigun bhajai. Brahmaa Vishnu Mahesh. Jaisaa guru jaako milai. Sailaa de updesh._ (Kabir says: people of three natures worship the three gunas — Brahma, Vishnu, and Mahesh. Whatever kind of guru one finds, accordingly he gives his teaching.)

Daas Kabirji says: people with three kinds of nature-traits worship the gods of three kinds of qualities — Brahma, Vishnu, and Shiva — that is, they worship these gods possessing the three gunas of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Whoever finds a guru of a particular nature is instructed by him to worship the deity possessing that corresponding quality.

_Gaji mam baasto. Tinko ek got. Jene jevaa gurumale. Taisaa neekasaa pot._ (This is my own experience — theirs is a single lineage: whatever kind of guru one finds, such is the fabric that comes out in the disciple.)

The composer of the couplet says: for me one or another kind of cloth has been prepared — cloth of any kind is still just called cloth, but whatever sort of craftsman-guru a given piece of cloth has found to weave it, it becomes cloth of that very sort, of good or of bad weave.

In the Samagam, Omkar has been called the baasto (the length of woven cloth). This baasto is the garment by which bondage is tied on. Thus the baasto is the body that the soul has received. The reckoning of one's lineage (gotra) runs according to the tradition of the guru-forefathers one has obtained, and accordingly one's pot — that is, one's nature and qualities — is formed.

_Koi puje dev deraan. Koi puje bam. Jene jevaa guru male. Tene tevi gam._ (Some worship the gods in the temple shrines, some worship Bam — Mahadev; whatever kind of guru one finds, such is the understanding one gets.)

Some people worship gods and goddesses in temples, while others worship Mahadev. Whatever sort of guru people find to give them instruction, they come to understand devotion to be practised accordingly.

_Ashvah shastram shastram veena vaani narashchanaari cha | Purushavisheshah praapta bhavantyayogyaashcha yogyaashcha ||119||_

Mitrabhed, Panchatantra: a horse, a weapon, a scripture, a veena, speech, a man and a woman — all of these, according to the sort of person into whose hands they come, turn out to be worthy or unworthy accordingly.
